blocks.text: 1. Dense Retrieval

blocks.alt: A chunk goes through dense embedding to produce a dense vector

blocks.text: Dense retrieval, covering the dense embedding based retrieval approach in more depth, revisits semantic search through the specific lens of its dense vector foundation.
It is another name for semantic search that emphasizes the dense vector representation underneath.
2. Revisiting Semantic Search By Another Name
Dense retrieval is the same technique as semantic search.
This topic revisits it through the lens of the dense embeddings specifically doing the work.
3. Why Dense Embeddings Dominate The Term
Dense embeddings capture semantic similarity because dense vectors excel at representing nuanced, contextual meaning.
That strength is why the retrieval community calls this approach dense retrieval.
4. Single Vector Representation Per Chunk

blocks.alt: A chunk maps to one fixed vector

blocks.text: Each chunk gets represented by exactly one dense vector.
That single vector has to capture the chunk's entire meaning at once.
5. Bi-Encoder Architecture

blocks.alt: A query goes through a query encoder while a document goes through a document encoder

blocks.text: Queries and chunks get embedded independently, each through its own pass of the same model.
This design, called a bi-encoder, allows chunk embeddings to be precomputed once, ahead of time.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Component","When it gets embedded"],"rows":[["Chunks","Once, ahead of time, during ingestion"],["Query","Fresh, at the moment of search"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Precomputing Chunk Embeddings

blocks.alt: All chunks get embeddings precomputed at index time

blocks.text: Every chunk's embedding gets computed once during ingestion, the same preprocessing pattern covered in Indexing.
Only the query embedding needs to be computed fresh at search time.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: The bi-encoder's ability to precompute chunk embeddings is exactly why dense retrieval can serve queries in milliseconds even against millions of chunks, since only the single query embedding needs fresh computation.

blocks.text: 7. Lossless Meaning Versus Lossy Compression

blocks.alt: Full text is compressed into a dense vector

blocks.text: Compressing a dense vector, as covered in Compression, trades some retrieval accuracy for storage savings.
Dense retrieval's quality depends directly on how much of that original signal survives.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Aggressively compressing dense embeddings for storage savings directly degrades dense retrieval's core strength, since the entire technique relies on the vector preserving nuanced meaning accurately.

blocks.text: 8. Dense Retrieval Limitations

blocks.alt: Dense retrieval is weak on exact terms and rare words

blocks.text: As with semantic search generally, exact term matching remains dense retrieval's persistent blind spot.
That gap is exactly why hybrid search exists.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Retrieval need","Dense retrieval fit"],"rows":[["Nuanced, conceptual meaning","Strong fit"],["Exact term or code matching","Weak fit, needs sparse retrieval or hybrid search"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Dense Retrieval Is The Right Foundation

blocks.alt: Needing a semantic retrieval foundation points toward dense retrieval

blocks.text: Nuanced, conceptual retrieval needs suit dense retrieval well.
Precision term matching requirements, by contrast, need sparse retrieval, covered as the next topic in this module.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates precomputing chunk embeddings once and embedding only the query fresh at search time.

code.content:
import time

chunks = [
    "How to reset your account password.",
    "Steps for updating billing information.",
    "Guide to changing notification preferences.",
]

def fake_dense_embed(text):
    # simulates the cost of a real dense embedding model call
    time.sleep(0.001)
    words = text.lower().split()
    return (len(words), sum(len(w) for w in words))

print("Precomputing chunk embeddings once, ahead of time:")
start = time.time()
chunk_embeddings = [fake_dense_embed(c) for c in chunks]
precompute_time = time.time() - start
print(f"  Precompute time for {len(chunks)} chunks: {precompute_time:.4f} seconds\n")

query = "how do I change my password"
print("Embedding only the query fresh at search time:")
start = time.time()
query_embedding = fake_dense_embed(query)
query_time = time.time() - start
print(f"  Query embedding time: {query_time:.4f} seconds")

print("\nAt search time, only the query needed fresh computation.")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows chunk embeddings computed once upfront, while the query embedding gets computed only at the moment of search, the bi-encoder architecture that keeps dense retrieval fast.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Recomputing chunk embeddings on every query instead of precomputing them once during ingestion.
Over compressing dense embeddings without measuring the resulting retrieval accuracy loss.
Relying on dense retrieval alone for queries that need exact term matching.
Treating dense retrieval as a different technique from semantic search rather than the same one.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Dense retrieval is another name for semantic search, emphasizing its dense vector foundation.
Dense vectors excel at representing nuanced, contextual meaning, giving the approach its name.
Each chunk gets represented by exactly one dense vector capturing its entire meaning at once.
A bi-encoder architecture embeds queries and chunks independently through the same model.
Chunk embeddings get precomputed once during ingestion; only the query needs fresh computation.
Compressing dense vectors trades accuracy for storage, directly affecting retrieval quality.
Exact term matching remains dense retrieval's persistent blind spot.
That blind spot is exactly why hybrid search combines it with sparse retrieval.
Next up: Sparse Retrieval, covering the exact term based retrieval approach in more depth.
